questions.asking: a small, precise error that separates people who have built dashboards from people who have read about them — percentiles do not average
questions.answer: Percentiles do not average. The mean of per-host p99s is not the fleet's p99 and has no statistical interpretation at all: a host serving ten requests contributes as much as one serving ten million, and the fleet's true p99 can sit outside the range of the per-host values entirely. Aggregate the underlying distribution instead — sum histogram buckets across hosts, then compute the quantile once. And track p50, p99 and p99.9 separately, per endpoint, splitting successful requests from failed ones, because fast errors otherwise flatter the number.
redFlags: sees nothing wrong with it
offers the max of the per-host p99s without noting that is a different statistic
no mention of histograms or of aggregating the distribution
does not separate error latency from success latency

followUps.q: Your traces show a 900 ms gap with no span in it. Where do you look?
followUps.answer: At an asynchronous boundary first, and at the clock second. Trace context dropped at a queue hop is the most common gap of all, and clock skew across hosts makes cross-host timestamps unreliable — rely on span durations rather than wall-clock differences, and make sure NTP is actually running.

followUps.q: You have excellent dashboards and a 40-pages-a-week rotation. What is the real problem?
followUps.answer: Alert fatigue, and it is a correctness problem rather than a comfort one — the responder has learned that the pager is noise and will miss the one that is not. Move cause alerts to tickets, page only on burn rate and user impact, put a runbook link on every page, and delete the dashboards nobody owns.

tracks.name: Architecture
tracks.blurb: Naming the bottleneck before drawing the box, and scaling one at a time

questions.q: A six-person team wants to split their monolith into eight microservices. What do you say?
questions.asking: whether they know microservices are an organisational solution to a team-scaling problem, and whether they do the availability arithmetic unprompted
questions.answer: No, and the arithmetic is the argument rather than my taste. Eight synchronous services at 99.9% each gives 0.999 to the eighth, about 99.2% — roughly 70 hours a year against the 8.8 they have now — and that is the optimistic figure, because it assumes independent failures and ignores the shared database, the retry storms and the deploys. Separately, six people cannot operate eight services: not should not, cannot. Each one carries a repository, a pipeline, a runtime to patch, dashboards, tuned alerts and a slot in somebody's head. Start with a modular monolith, which is the default and is not a compromise.
redFlags: reaches for microservices before naming a bottleneck
claims microservices are faster
does no availability arithmetic
treats monolith as a synonym for unstructured

followUps.q: They say the monolith is a tangle and the network will force the boundaries. Respond.
followUps.answer: What they want to escape is a ball of mud, and there are three options rather than two — the middle one is a modular monolith with boundaries enforced by the compiler, package visibility and architecture tests. If you cannot maintain module boundaries in one process you will not maintain them across a network; you will have the same tangle with worse latency and no stack traces. Do it in the monolith, where a violation is a build failure instead of an incident.

followUps.q: What would actually justify a split?
followUps.answer: A named, specific constraint — most often two teams measurably and repeatedly blocking each other on releases. Otherwise a genuinely divergent scaling profile where the divergent part is separable, a divergent availability requirement across an asynchronous boundary, or regulatory data residency. Notice how many of those are about organisations, contracts and legislation rather than about computers.

questions.q: Walk me through scaling a read-heavy web application from one server to a hundred times the traffic.
questions.asking: whether they scale one bottleneck at a time and name what each change cost, or recite a finished architecture they have seen in a diagram
questions.answer: One bottleneck at a time, naming the cost of each. Start with client, server, database, and say plainly what rps that is correct up to and what saturates first. Then: fix the queries and add indexes, routinely 10-100x and free; scale up, which needs no architectural change; make the app tier stateless and put a redundant pair of load balancers in front; add a shared cache if and only if access is skewed, which buys staleness and invalidation; add read replicas, which buy read scale and introduce lag and the read-your-writes bug; move slow work behind a queue, which removes backpressure. Sharding is last and is close to irreversible — most systems never leave the first three steps.
redFlags: draws the finished architecture in the first five minutes
adds a cache before demonstrating the bottleneck
no number anywhere in the answer
a single load balancer in a design sold as highly available

followUps.q: You put the load balancer in so no single machine can take the site down. How many single points of failure does the system now have?
followUps.answer: At least one and probably three. The load balancer itself, unless it is a redundant pair — five servers behind one balancer is a system with the availability of one machine. DNS is now on the critical path too, and the five servers almost certainly share one database. Three app servers in front of one primary has the primary's availability; redundancy at the wrong layer buys nothing.

followUps.q: At which step did you first buy a new failure mode, and what is it?
followUps.answer: The cache. It is the first component whose absence changes behaviour rather than capacity: at a 95% hit rate, losing it sends a 20x step change at the database in a single instant. That is how a cache outage becomes a full outage, and the cache is usually still labelled safe to lose on the diagram.

questions.q: How do you tell whether a team has microservices or a distributed monolith?
questions.asking: whether they have a measurable diagnostic rather than an aesthetic judgement
questions.answer: One question: how many services must be released together for a typical feature? If the answer is greater than one, it is a distributed monolith — and it is worth charting monthly, because it is the single best architectural health metric available. The corroborating symptoms: one feature touches four repositories, services share a database schema, you cannot run or test one service alone, and release order matters and is written down somewhere, which means deployment has become a distributed transaction performed by humans. A distributed monolith is worse than a monolith on every axis, and there is no benefit column.
redFlags: judges by the number of services
counts a shared database as a service boundary
offers no measurable diagnostic
would never consider merging services back together

followUps.q: Three of those symptoms are present. What is the correct response?
followUps.answer: Usually to merge services back together. Nobody wants to and it is almost always right — recognising a wrong boundary and undoing it is a sign of competence rather than failure. Check also whether the split came with a reorganisation, because adopting microservices without reorganising is a rename: team boundaries are a physical fact and repository boundaries are a suggestion.

followUps.q: Where should the line have gone?
followUps.answer: Where the transactions are. If two operations must be atomic they belong in the same service — splitting an invariant buys you a saga with explicit compensating actions for every failure point, plus eventual consistency and reconciliation, forever. The classic mistake is one service per noun, User and Order and Product, which guarantees chatty synchronous fan-out and split invariants.

questions.q: A team proposes building a release-orchestration tool so their twelve services deploy in the correct order. Do you fund it?
questions.asking: whether they can spot a tool that automates a symptom and thereby entrenches the disease
questions.answer: No. Release order mattering is the diagnostic for a distributed monolith, and a tool that makes the ordering reliable removes the pain that would otherwise force the real fix. The problem is compatibility, not orchestration: apply expand-contract to the service interfaces so any version can run beside any other, and the ordering question disappears. Note that during a rolling deploy old and new code are already both running, so every change has to be backwards compatible for the length of the rollout regardless.
redFlags: funds it because it reduces incidents this quarter
treats deploy ordering as a normal operational cost
no mention of backwards compatibility or expand-contract
cannot name what the tool would be hiding

followUps.q: Twelve synchronous services at 99.9% each. What have they actually got?
followUps.answer: 0.999 to the twelfth, about 98.8%, which is over four days of downtime a year — before counting deploys, and deploys cause most outages. Twelve services that are each individually excellent give an application that is not, and nobody is at fault: no team missed its SLO, the architecture did this on its own.

followUps.q: Name the only three things that break that multiplication.
followUps.answer: Make the hop asynchronous, which is the single most effective availability intervention in a service architecture. Make the dependency optional and degrade, because a dependency you can fall back from is not in the product. Or cache its answers and accept the staleness. Retries, circuit breakers and bulkheads limit the blast radius; they do not remove the term.

questions.q: A worker fleet drains a two-hour backlog into the same primary database that serves user traffic. Autoscaling is keyed on queue depth, which is correct. The website goes down. Walk the mechanism.
questions.asking: whether they can compose four individually reasonable decisions into one outage — the class of failure no single-component page can teach
questions.answer: Four things compose, and each was individually reasonable. Moving work behind a queue removed the natural backpressure the request path had: on the request path a slow database slows the client, which throttles arrival, and behind a queue nothing pushes back. Depth is the right autoscaling signal and it is also what aims the fleet at the database, because depth is enormous so the policy adds workers until it is not. The number that decides the outcome is total fleet concurrency — workers times per-worker concurrency — and nobody set it: twenty workers at concurrency 50 is a thousand simultaneous operations, configured by two people in two files. Finally the connection pool is shared with the request path, so it exhausts and the site returns errors while the database itself sits comfortably idle.
redFlags: blames the autoscaler and switches the signal to CPU
reads the idle database CPU as evidence the database is healthy
no mention of fleet concurrency being a product of two numbers
believes the queue added capacity

followUps.q: What do you change?
followUps.answer: Bound total fleet concurrency against measured downstream capacity and cap the autoscaler's maximum to respect it. Give workers their own connection pool so neither workload can starve the other. And accept that the drain now takes longer, because the backlog has no user waiting on it and the website does.

followUps.q: State the general shape in one sentence.
followUps.answer: A queue does not add capacity, it moves the moment you pay for the shortfall. Two correct components and one bad interaction — and the asymmetry underneath it is that the request path passes through three implicit limits before reaching the database, a load balancer, a sized pool and clients that time out and give up, while the worker path passes through none of them.
